newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Peacekeepers say Liberia on course for polls.
newsitem.headline: Peacekeepers say Liberia on course for polls.

text.p: The commander of the ECOMOG peacekeeping force in Liberia said on Monday disarmament of guerrillas in the West African country had largely been completed and elections should be held in May as scheduled.
"We have just completed the disarmament and demobilisation phases," General Victor Malu told West African army chiefs of staff at a review meeting in Monrovia.

Malu said the Nigerian-led force sent to Liberia in 1990 by the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) was turning its focus to elections, the final stage of a regional peace programme to bring Liberia out of a seven-year conflict.

"With the successes achieved in the just concluded phase we have begun to see the light at the end of the tunnel. Liberians and all parties to this conflict have completly demonstrated their resolve to end this fraticidal crisis," he said.
Malu told Reuters that 91 percent of armed guerrillas had turned in their weapons by last Friday's end of a voluntary disarmament period and the country was safe for elections.
"We will be recommending elections nationwide," he said.
But the ECOMOG force still needed troop reinforcements promised by some of the 16 ECOWAS members to provide more security in populated areas and to hunt down armed guerrillas still holding out.
The two-day chiefs of staff meeting will assess the security situation and advise foreign ministers from a nine-nation committee on Liberia who hold their own talks on Thursday and Friday.

Diplomats and military sources said they expect they will advise that presidential and legislative elections be held in May as planned despite reservations by United Nations and some other electoral experts about preparations for voting.

After several failed accords to end civil war that has killed more than 150,000 people, warring parties committed themselves to a last-chance deal signed in the Nigerian capital Abuja last August, setting a new truce and political timetable.
The United States expects to give up to $6 million for the elections and its ambassador in Monrovia, William Milan, expects the election timetable to be maintained.

"I would be surprisd if they decided not to go ahead with the elctions," Milan told Reuters. "I believe ECOWAS is committed to the Abuja schedule. I think that the United States and the other donors and supporting countries are also committed to that schedule."
He acknowledged lingering security worries due to isolated incidents of armed attacks and harassment but added: "We all believe that while security is not perfect, it is going to get much better."
Chief warlord Charles Taylor who started civil war in 1989 has practically launched his presidential election campaign and has given a warning of trouble if voting is delayed.
